title: Future and CompletableFuture
summary: Future is a blocking read-handle; CompletableFuture is a composable, manually-completable pipeline. Know when to chain, which executor runs each stage, and where exceptions go.

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: **`Future` is a ticket you block on. `CompletableFuture` is a pipeline you compose.** If your code calls `get()` in the middle of a request path, you kept the old bottleneck and just renamed the class. Use `CompletableFuture` only when you chain with `thenApply` / `thenCompose` / `thenCombine`, handle failure in the chain with `exceptionally` / `handle`, and control *where* each stage runs. The trade-off every time: composition buys throughput and expressiveness, but forces you to reason about executors, exception propagation, and who completes the future.

`Future<V>` — since Java 5 — is a minimal read-only handle for a computation owned by someone else. The interface is five methods and nothing more: `get()`, `get(timeout, unit)`, `isDone()`, `isCancelled()`, and `cancel(mayInterruptIfRunning)`. You get one from `ExecutorService.submit(Callable)`. You cannot complete it yourself, you cannot attach a callback to it, and you cannot combine two of them except by blocking on both. That limitation is intentional: it models delegation to a thread pool, not a dataflow graph. If you need the result, you park the calling thread until it arrives.

`CompletableFuture<V>` — since Java 8 — implements both `Future<V>` and `CompletionStage<V>`. That second interface is the whole point: ~50 methods for building dependent computations without blocking. It is writable from any thread via `complete(value)`, `completeExceptionally(ex)`, `cancel()`, and `obtrudeValue()`, and readable via chained stages like `thenApply`, `thenAccept`, `thenRun`, `thenCompose`, `thenCombine`, `allOf`, `anyOf`, `orTimeout`, plus explicit error stages `exceptionally`, `handle`, and `whenComplete`. You create one either implicitly with `supplyAsync` / `runAsync`, or explicitly with `new CompletableFuture()` and complete it later — for example when a callback, NIO completion handler, or message listener fires. That is why it is both a future *and* a promise: the consumer chains, the producer completes.

`Future` forces three bad habits at scale. First, result retrieval is blocking-only: there is no `onComplete` hook, so fan-out code becomes `future1.get(); future2.get();` in sequence and latency adds instead of overlapping. Second, there is no composition: you cannot say *fetch user, then fetch orders for that user* without waking a thread just to submit the next task. Third, errors are invisible until `get()` throws `ExecutionException`, so timeout, fallback, and retry logic lives outside the computation as nested `try/catch` around blocking calls. The design choice was to keep `Future` dumb and leave orchestration to the caller. The trade-off: simple contract and easy cancellation, in exchange for one thread parked per in-flight dependency and no declarative pipeline. That is exactly what `CompletableFuture` was added to fix — at the cost of a far larger API surface and subtler threading semantics.

Think of `Future` as polling a mailbox and `CompletableFuture` as wiring callbacks to that mailbox. With `ExecutorService.submit`, the pool wraps your `Callable` in a `FutureTask`, runs it, stores the outcome, and unparks any thread stuck in `get()`. Nothing else happens automatically. With `CompletableFuture`, completion is an event: when the upstream stage finishes, the runtime schedules each dependent stage according to its variant. The non-`Async` variant (`thenApply`) runs in the thread that completed the parent — cheap, but it hijacks that thread. The `Async` variant (`thenApplyAsync(fn, executor)`) hands off to the supplied executor — safer for blocking or slow stages, but adds a queue hop. No executor argument means `ForkJoinPool.commonPool`, which is the source of half the production incidents with this API. The mechanism to internalise: completion triggers scheduling, and scheduling needs an explicit executor decision every time.

blocks.text: The sync-vs-async suffix is the control knob interviewers probe. `thenApply` inherits the completer thread: good for pure CPU transforms under a microsecond, dangerous if the function blocks on I/O or takes 200ms, because you stall the I/O thread or the common pool worker that just finished the parent. `thenApplyAsync(fn, myPool)` isolates that cost to `myPool` — which is why you should pass an explicit executor for anything that touches sockets, disks, or locks. Trade-off stated plainly: same-thread chaining minimises latency and context switches; executor-hopped chaining preserves isolation and prevents pool starvation. Defaulting to the two-argument `Async` overload with a named pool is the only defensible default in server code.

blocks.caption: Honest trade-offs between the two APIs.
rows: Completion
Only the executor completes it. Simple ownership, no manual completion.
Anyone can complete it. Flexible for callbacks and adapters, but ownership is unclear — leaks and double-completion are your bug.
Composition
None. Sequence with blocking get(). Easy to read, wastes threads.
thenApply / thenCompose / thenCombine / allOf / anyOf. No parked threads, but pipeline ordering and executor choice must be reasoned about.
Error handling
ExecutionException on get(). Explicit but far from the failure site.
exceptionally / handle / whenComplete in-chain. Localises recovery, but silently swallowing exceptions is one typo away.
Threading
Caller blocks; worker runs. Predictable, low surprise.
Dependent may run on completer thread, commonPool, or custom pool. Fast when correct, pool-exhaustion when wrong.
Cancellation
cancel(true) interrupts the worker if running. Well understood.
cancel() completes exceptionally with CancellationException and cascades to dependents. Interruption of running stages is not guaranteed — must check cooperative cancellation.

blocks.text: How it fails in production, and the symptom you would see

`CompletableFuture` failures rarely throw in your face; they stall, default silently, or complete the wrong branch. The signature in dashboards is thread starvation with low CPU: request latency p99 spikes while worker pools look idle, because threads are parked in `get()` / `join()` or the common pool is saturated by blocking stages. The second signature is wrong data, not errors: an `exceptionally` that returns a default poisons downstream stages that cannot tell fallback from real. The third is lost work: a future nobody joins and whose exception nobody observes fails silently until a customer reports missing side effects. Always name the executor, always bound waits with `orTimeout`, and always log in `whenComplete` before you recover.

blocks.caption: Failure modes you must be able to diagnose from symptoms.
rows: Common-pool saturation
Sudden latency cliff across unrelated endpoints, ForkJoinPool threads BLOCKED on socket read
Blocking I/O inside thenApply or supplyAsync without executor. Fix: dedicated pools for blocking vs CPU; use Async overload with explicit executor.
Blocking get() in event loop
Throughput collapses under load, thread dump shows request threads parked in Future.get
Sequential get() defeats async overlap. Fix: compose with thenCombine / allOf and block once at the edge, or return the future upstream.
Swallowed exception via exceptionally
200 OK with empty or stale payload, no error logs
exceptionally returning default for all throwables including bugs. Fix: handle only expected types, log and rethrow the rest via completeExceptionally.
Nested futures from thenApply
Type is CompletableFuture of CompletableFuture, join returns inner future object not value
Used thenApply where thenCompose was needed for dependent async call. Fix: thenCompose for future-returning functions; thenApply for pure mappings.
Unobserved failure / no join
Missing writes, metrics gaps, no stack trace
Fire-and-forget chain with no terminal join and no whenComplete. Fix: always terminate with join at edge and attach logging stage; consider orTimeout.

blocks.title: The default-executor trap
blocks.text: `supplyAsync(task)` and `thenApplyAsync(fn)` with no executor use `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, sized to CPUs minus one and shared with parallel streams. Put a 50ms downstream HTTP call there and 32 concurrent requests exhaust it. Interviewers expect you to say: **never rely on the default in server code — inject a named ThreadPoolExecutor for I/O and keep CPU transforms inline or on a CPU pool.** Name the trade-off: one extra constructor parameter buys isolation and debuggability.
Code that makes the difference visible

This is the baseline you must be able to write cold. It is correct for two parallel calls, and that is its ceiling. The `get(timeout)` is non-negotiable — unbounded `get()` is how one slow dependency wedges every request thread. The trade-off is explicit: you get per-task cancellation and a readable sequence, but the calling thread contributes zero work while parked. With ten downstream calls the thread-park cost dominates, and error handling is disconnected from the stage that failed. That is the cue to switch APIs, not to add more threads.

Why this shape wins: `supplyAsync` with `ioPool` isolates blocking DAO calls off the common pool — isolation over brevity. `thenComposeAsync` is chosen because the second fetch *depends* on the first and itself returns a future; `thenApply` here would nest futures instead of flattening them. `thenCombine` overlaps independent work without manual thread juggling. `orTimeout` bounds each leg so one slow shard cannot hold the merge forever. `whenComplete` logs the real cause *before* `exceptionally` substitutes a fallback, which prevents silent data corruption. The single `join()` at the edge is deliberate: unchecked, but safe here because failure was already mapped to a fallback. Trade-off: you eliminated thread parking in the middle at the cost of having to justify every executor and every error-mapping decision.
How it shows up in an interview

items.title: Write the Future baseline first
items.text: Submit two Callables, get with timeout, cancel on failure, shutdown the pool. They check timeout handling and interrupt propagation before anything fancy.

items.title: Convert to a non-blocking chain
items.text: Replace sequential get() with supplyAsync plus thenApply for pure transforms and thenCompose for dependent async calls. Say aloud why thenCompose flattens and thenApply maps — mixing them up is an instant fail.

items.title: Fan-out and merge
items.text: Combine independent futures with thenCombine for two, allOf plus join for N. Explain that allOf does not give you values — you still join each constituent after it completes — and that anyOf is for hedged or fastest-wins reads.

items.title: Design the error and time policy
items.text: Add orTimeout per stage, handle vs exceptionally with justification, and a whenComplete log tap. State what is retried, what falls back, and what propagates. Vague exceptionally(return null) answers lose points.

items.title: Defend the executor topology
items.text: Propose one bounded pool for blocking I/O, keep CPU maps inline, size queues and set RejectedExecutionHandler explicitly. Explain why commonPool is rejected for I/O and how you would prove starvation from a thread dump.

items: `CompletableFuture` is automatically faster — it is not. Without overlap or isolation it adds scheduling overhead to the same blocking work.
Non-Async stages run on a background thread — no, they run on the completing thread. Only `Async` variants schedule elsewhere.
The no-arg `Async` overload is safe — it hits the shared common pool. In a service, always pass an explicit executor.
`allOf` returns combined values — it returns `Void`. You must `join()` each original future after `allOf` completes.
`exceptionally` and `handle` are interchangeable — `exceptionally` only sees failures; `handle` sees value or failure and can transform both.
`cancel(true)` reliably stops a chained pipeline — it completes the future exceptionally but does not guarantee interruption of an already-running stage.

blocks.caption: Selection guide: optimise for thread parking vs orchestration cost.
rows: Single background task, result needed inline
Future with get(timeout)
No pipeline to build; blocking once is simpler and easier to cancel.
Parallel fan-out merged at request edge
CompletableFuture + thenCombine / allOf
Overlaps latency without parking one thread per dependency.
Dependent async steps (id -> orders -> profile)
thenCompose chain
Flattens future-of-future and keeps error context in one pipeline.
Callback or NIO completion must drive logic
Manually completed CompletableFuture
Future cannot be completed externally; CompletableFuture bridges callback and chain worlds.
Bulk CPU transforms with structured lifetime
ExecutorService + Future or virtual threads
Pipeline machinery adds nothing; prefer simple submit/join or scoped concurrency.

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: `Future` is a blocking ticket for one task; `CompletableFuture` is a manually-completable pipeline with `thenApply` for maps, `thenCompose` for dependent async calls, `thenCombine` / `allOf` for fan-out, in-chain error handling, and — critically — an explicit executor per blocking stage so you never starve the common pool.
